blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Request threads add metric names to one shared StringBuffer `body` with `if (body.length() > 0) body.append(','); body.append(name);`. The buffer is empty when two threads add `cpu` and `mem` at the same moment. What can `body` hold afterwards?

options.text: `cpumem` is possible, since the other thread's append can run between one thread's length() and its own append
options.says: each StringBuffer call holds the lock only while it runs, so both threads can read length 0 before either appends

options.text: `cpumem` is possible, since the second thread's length() can read a stale 0 that the first thread's append never published
options.says: every StringBuffer method is synchronized on the buffer, so a call sees what earlier calls wrote; the gap is between the calls, not stale data

options.text: Only `cpu,mem` or `mem,cpu` is possible, since every method of a StringBuffer is synchronized on the same buffer
options.says: synchronized methods make each call atomic, not the check followed by the appends

options.text: Only `cpu,mem` or `mem,cpu` is possible, since the JIT merges the length check and the appends into one locked region
options.says: lock coarsening is an optimisation the JIT may apply, not a guarantee, and an interpreted or differently compiled run interleaves

origin.section: StringBuffer Locks Each Call, So a Line Built from Several Calls Still Interleaves

questions.stem: A changelog page builds its newest-first text with `for (Entry e : entries) view.insert(0, e.line());` on one StringBuilder. With 30,000 entries the loop takes 60 ms. Roughly how long will it take with 120,000 entries of the same size?

options.text: About a second, since every insert shifts all the characters already in the builder
options.says: the work per insert grows with the text so far, so four times the entries is about sixteen times the time

options.text: About a second, since the builder allocates a new, larger array for every insert
options.says: the builder grows to about twice its capacity only when the text doesn't fit, so allocation stays linear

options.text: About a quarter of a second, since an insert copies characters only when the array has to grow
options.says: that is true of appending at the end; an insert at the front moves every character after it on each call

options.text: About a quarter of a second, since each line is written into the builder once, whatever its position
options.says: each line is written once, but every later insert at the front moves it again

origin.section: A Builder Is an Array: Growing It and Inserting at the Front Copy What Is Already There

questions.stem: Each pool thread of a render service keeps a StringBuilder in a ThreadLocal; for each page it calls setLength(0), appends the page and returns toString(). A heap dump taken while no page is being rendered shows dozens of byte arrays of several megabytes. What are they most likely to be?

options.text: The builders' arrays, each sized by the biggest page its thread built, since clearing the text keeps the array
options.says: setLength(0) leaves the array as it is, so each builder keeps the capacity its largest page needed for as long as its thread lives

options.text: The builders' arrays, each sized by the last page its thread built, since clearing the text resets the capacity
options.says: setLength(0) changes only the length; the capacity stays at the largest size the builder reached, until trimToSize() or a new builder

options.text: The Strings' arrays from the pages built, since toString() hands the builder's array to the String
options.says: toString() copies the text into a new String on every call, so no String shares the builder's array

options.text: The Strings' arrays from the pages built, since a String from toString() is as large as the capacity
options.says: toString() copies only the characters in use, so the String is the size of its text

origin.section: setLength(0) Empties a Builder and Keeps Its Array

questions.stem: An alerting job keeps `Set<StringBuilder> sent = new HashSet<>()`. It builds each alert's text in a new StringBuilder and notifies on-call only `if (sent.add(text))`. The same check fails twice in a row, producing the text `disk /var 91%` both times. What does on-call get?

options.text: Two notifications, since the second builder is a different object and the set compares objects
options.says: StringBuilder inherits equals and hashCode from Object, so two builders with the same text are different set entries

options.text: Two notifications, since the first builder's hash code changed as text was appended to it
options.says: a builder's hash code is Object's, which doesn't depend on its text, so appending doesn't change it

options.text: One notification, since the set compares the two builders' text with compareTo
options.says: HashSet uses equals and hashCode; compareTo compares text but the set never calls it

options.text: One notification, since the set compares the two builders' text through their equals
options.says: StringBuilder doesn't override equals, so equals is true only for the same object

origin.section: Two Builders Are Equal Only When They Are the Same Object

concepts: StringBuilder and StringBuffer inherit equals and hashCode from Object, so two builders with the same text are different set entries; content is compared with compareTo, contentEquals or toString().
A builder that runs out of room grows to the larger of what is needed and twice its capacity plus 2 by copying, so appending stays linear and sizing it to the result avoids the growth garbage.
insert at the front shifts every character already in the builder on every call, so a loop of front inserts takes time that grows with the square of the count.
A check of a StringBuffer followed by an append is two locked calls, so another thread can act between them.
